keyFindings.description: Security[secret]: round 2's finding 3 is half fixed. The paragraph says what exit 0 covers, which is the part I asked for and is right. Its gate on what to do before storing credential material is unsound, and it waves through the one case where a peer is known to be behind. The instruction is 'read the broker's log for those lines since the retag, and if any names your secret, or if you cannot read the log, wait five minutes'. Of the three lines it enumerates, only one carries the secret: 'broker: the other pods were not told to reread a secret' logs secret=name (main.go:427-430). The redial line logs channels, error, attempt and wait_ms and no secret (pglisten/listener.go:126-127), and the catch-up line logs error alone (main.go:348), as does the bind's 'binding before the reread listener has had an answer' (main.go:361), which the paragraph does not list at all. So an operator who reads the log, sees a pod redialing, and applies the gate literally concludes that no line names the secret and stores the App key at once — in exactly the state the paragraph exists to catch. It also omits the one further line that does name a secret, 'broker: a notification's reread of a secret did not run secret=… sender=…' (reread/reread.go:175), which is the most direct evidence that a named peer is stale for that name. And five minutes is presented as the safe wait: the next reload is another whole-namespace listing read, and the store's listing lags a write by up to 5 minutes on AWS and 6 hours on Secret Manager (secrets/aws.go:72-77, secrets/gcp.go:185-192, the limitation main.go:333-335 records and dispatch://INFRA-375 tracks), so on Secret Manager that wait is not a bound at all. Remedy, in the prose this change already adds and not in code: gate on any of those lines appearing since the retag rather than on one naming the secret, list the two lines that name a secret and the three that do not, and do not present the reload interval as a convergence bound where the store's own lag exceeds it.

The alarm table contradicts itself within four rows. The redial row says in bold 'This is the only signal that a pod's fan-out is dead', and the rows at :366-369 document three more: 'broker: serving without the boot's catch-up policy load…' (added this round), 'broker: the other pods were not told to reread a secret' and 'broker: a notification's reread of a secret did not run'. Each of those is a pod outside the fan-out for at least one name. The claim was true when the redial line was the only one; this round added the fourth and left the word 'only' standing.

Two statements in the first-load comment overstate what the code does, both about the path that returns at :267-269. ':243-245' says a pod signalled mid-boot 'finishes that load before it drains'; it finishes the load and then returns without draining at all, which is what :265-266 argues for. ':265-266' then says binding and running a shutdown budget for a server that never served 'would hold the pod open for over a minute': shutdownTimeout is a maximum rather than a wait, and srv.Shutdown on a server with nothing in flight returns at once, so the figure describes a bound and not a duration anyone would pay.

secondSignalFindsServing's comment claims more than the function establishes. It reads serveStarted and returns; its caller logs and calls os.Exit(1) afterwards (main.go:123-136), with nothing ordering that exit against main closing serveStarted at :481 and starting srv.Serve. So 'it has served nothing' is the state at the observation rather than at the exit. This is far narrower than the defect it replaces — the old shape was a coin flip between two ready cases, measured at 39 of 100 on the honest signal pair, and this window is between a function returning and the next two statements — and I am not asking for a synchronisation. The comment and the log line should say what is established: that the broker had not begun serving when the second signal was read.

The row's comment does not describe the fixture it builds. It says 'each goroutine's first call also opens its pooled connection', which is how it accounts for 14.7 ms and 6.3 ms against a contention it measures elsewhere at 0.7-1.6 ms; store.Open pings the pool before returning (store/store.go:81-84, reached through storetest.Open at storetest.go:99), so a warmed connection already exists when the goroutines start. It also frames the fixture as 'a cold two-pod boot runs oauthstore.Store.Secret on both pods', while both goroutines share one oauthStore over one pool (:37), which is one pod's shape rather than two. The assertion is a quarter-of-the-bound margin and is unaffected either way; what is wrong is the comment's account of its own numbers, in the one row whose purpose is to make those numbers mean something.

measurementCorrection: My round-2 figure of 2 of 300, and the 10 of 300 I added from the tester's first real-binary run, were both measured with two back-to-back SIGTERMs. A pending non-realtime signal is not queued, so the kernel merges them and that harness often delivers one signal and never reaches the branch. The honest pair is SIGTERM then SIGINT, both in the broker's Notify set and unable to merge: 39 of 100 on the same pre-fix binary. Both of my figures were lower bounds and the bias runs one way only. Corrected on the finding-1 thread with the original left standing as the record, and in the pull request body's Look at first, which now carries each figure's method.
roundTwoFindingsVerified: Finding 1 closed and driven. secondSignalFindsServing (main.go:552-562) takes both signals and then reads serveStarted with a select/default, so the decision is the state at the check rather than a choice between two ready cases; a true answer hands over on the buffered drainNow the drain selects on (main.go:121,126,509), and the watchdog is again's only reader. TestASecondSignalAtAServingBrokerAlwaysDrains answers drain 500 of 500 where an overlay carrying the previous body answers exit 245 of 500, and the real binary drains 300 of 300 with the long-drain control still ending early at 0.03 s against 30 s and a one-signal control clean at 100.

Finding 2 closed to the invariant rather than to the window. The catch-up load (main.go:347) runs on the firstListen branch only, after pglisten has run OnConnected, which it does only once the LISTEN statement has returned, and before net.Listen — so the subscription exists before the read whose result it must invalidate. The timeout branch deliberately takes no catch-up, which is right: with no subscription there is nothing to order a read after. A failed catch-up warns and serves, the first load having succeeded. I checked the comment's claims against the code rather than reading them: policy.Current.Refresh, its recent anchors and Store.ListLag all exist and behave as it describes (policy/current.go:14-40,80-134).

The four stale statements of round 2 are fixed and the fixes are accurate: operate.md:269 now reads ten, AGENTS.md:2456-2465 now describes OnConnected and the catch-up load, AGENTS.md:3023-3028 now describes the unconditional registration and the single watchdog reader, and limits.go:194-201 now credits the replica count rather than the fan-out with multiplying the reloads, miss-path rereads and releases.
